A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AMIS study. The main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocations, additions and removals.

before.justification: V1 reports original jailbreak evaluations, including ASR and StrongREJECT results on AdvBench, JBB-Behaviors and HarmBench, alongside ablations and transfer experiments.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark evaluations and adds cross-dataset transfer, evaluator sensitivity, optimization controls and additional baseline experiments.

M1.justification: The core AMIS optimization loops, alignment objective, prompt inheritance and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Appendix B.8 adds a procedural extension using ActorBreaker as the inner loop coupled to AMIS scoring-template optimization.

E1.justification: V1's evaluation on 200 HarmBench behaviors disappears (B.6, Table 12); retaining the HarmBench judging prompt does not retain that dataset evaluation. V2 adds a distinct cross-dataset scenario transferring optimized scoring templates between AdvBench and JBB-Behaviors without further adaptation (Section 4.3, Table 6).

E2.justification: The main comparator set is retained, but v2 adds evaluated comparisons with Rainbow Teaming and ActorBreaker across several iteration budgets or attacker models (B.7, Table 14). Table 15 also introduces iterative ActorBreaker controls for comparison with the AMIS integration. These evaluated comparisons were absent from v1.

E3.justification: New experiments vary optimizer and judge models, scoring ranges, normalization and alignment-label subsets. They introduce extended inner-loop settings, frozen-template transfer and FN/ROUGE/BLEU diagnostics. The cost comparison now explicitly reports extending PAIR's iterations. Appendix I.1 replaces the displayed 1–10 ASR rubric with Yes/No instructions; this is a documented protocol correction, not evidence that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds cross-dataset generalization, optimizer/judge sensitivity, alignment-objective ablations, stronger inner-loop controls, ActorBreaker integration tests, template-evolution diagnostics and false-positive case studies. Conversely, v1's initial-prefix quality cases and five-versus-ten inherited-prompt analysis are removed. Existing component ablations and cross-model transfer analyses remain.

E5.justification: V1 B.5 and Table 11 report three repeated experiments with means and standard deviations for AMIS and PAIR, including ASR 87.3 ± 2.1 and 56.0 ± 1.8. V2 removes this section and its uncertainty estimates without replacement. Its mention of randomized Rainbow Teaming seed lists supplies no comparable uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1–5 retain their numerical values. V2 adds substantial results, including transfer ASRs of 86% and 87% (Table 6) and extended-inner-loop comparisons of 92% versus 96% ASR (Table 13), plus evaluator, baseline and template diagnostics. V1 Tables 9–12 disappear. V2 also incorrectly changes AuT's stated StR ranking from second-best to best, although Table 5 still reports 0.28 versus 0.41 for the ASR template.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, including Equations 1–8 and the ASR alignment definition, is retained. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs; v2's new diagnostics and parameter variations are empirical analyses.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contribution: jointly optimizing jailbreak prompts and scoring templates through meta-optimization. The headline state-of-the-art claims, including 88.0% ASR on Claude-3.5-Haiku and 100.0% on Claude-4-Sonnet, are unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of cross-dataset generalization, applicability with weaker optimizers/evaluators and template-calibration dynamics. Appendix H.1 identifies keyword, dual-use and structural-detail causes of false positives and discusses their safety tradeoff. Interpretations accompanying removed prefix/inheritance studies disappear. Some new interpretations overstate the evidence: Appendix E claims monotonically declining FN rates despite fluctuations in Figure 8.

D1.justification: V1 promises a future code release; v2 supplies a repository address and states that code is publicly available. V2 provides explicit binary ASR instructions, while the rubric previously labeled ASR reappears as a first-iteration scoring template. It also adds baseline implementation sources, translation and budget details, identifies default appendix evaluation settings, and supplies further intermediate templates.

R1.justification: The reference list and Related Works section retain the same cited works and central positioning. Appendix B.7–B.8 expands the relationship to previously cited Rainbow Teaming and ActorBreaker, particularly positioning AMIS as complementary to distribution-shift red-teaming through integration with ActorBreaker.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main methodological narrative remain intact. Changes include grammar and terminology edits, the conference header and acknowledgments, reorganization of Appendix B, and relocation of cost analysis into Section 4.3. Most expansion consists of new scientific content rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: V2 adds transfer, sensitivity and baseline tables, alignment/FN plots and failure-case figures, while removing v1 Tables 9–12. The cost plot moves into the main text and is redrawn with a per-query cost axis. Appendix prompt figures are reformatted as numbered listings with revised styling and wrapping; existing benchmark tables and transfer heatmaps are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 better tests dependence on evaluator choice and inner-loop strength, adds cross-dataset transfer and explicit failure analysis, and resolves the appendix's binary-ASR prompt mismatch while reporting code availability. These changes improve assessability and reproducibility. The net improvement is limited by removal of three-run uncertainty estimates and HarmBench dataset results, together with new claims contradicted by Table 5 and Figure 8.
